headline: Your digital game library is licensed, not owned, with publishers able to revoke access or shut down servers
summary: Publishers like 2K are shutting down servers for single-player modes, and even physical copies are becoming download codes, fundamentally changing what it means to 'buy' a game.
details: Major digital storefronts sell games as revocable licenses, not outright purchases. This means the terms of play are set by the company, and access can be withdrawn, impacting players' long-term game access.

For instance, NBA 2K25's MyCareer mode will become unplayable after December 31, 2026, when 2K shuts down its online servers. Despite paying $99.99 for the All-Star Edition, players get just over two years of access to this core single-player feature.

While delisting a game from storefronts still allows existing owners to redownload it, a server shutdown is more severe. Any game modes or features reliant on publisher servers cease to function, even for single-player experiences.

The most extreme scenario is a revoked license, where a game is entirely removed from a player's library. Ubisoft did this with The Crew in March 2024, reportedly deleting the always-online racer from player accounts and making it unplayable.

Platform rules are also evolving; PlayStation's license agreement states software is 'licensed to you, not sold.' Sony argued in a 2026 court filing that 'reasonable consumers' understand this distinction, highlighting the fragility of digital game 'ownership'.

Sony will transition to digital-only PlayStation games starting January 2028, ending disc-based releases for new titles. This shift further solidifies the digital licensing model, with physical boxes potentially containing only download codes, as seen with Grand Theft Auto VI.

Even physical discs don't guarantee perpetual access, as demonstrated by The Crew. Its disc version also stopped working when Ubisoft's servers were shut down, due to its constant online connection requirement.

Nintendo's Switch 2 is also moving towards game-key cards that require an initial download and online check-in. In contrast, GOG offers offline installers, allowing customers to keep and play games without needing ongoing store permission.

California's AB 2426 law, effective January 2025, mandates disclosure that customers receive a license, not ownership, when buying digital games. However, it doesn't prevent publishers from eventually taking games offline, and its enforcement is currently under litigation.

headline_marked: [[Ukraine builds combat robots]] to hunt Russian troops in underground gas pipelines
headline: Ukraine builds combat robots to hunt Russian troops in underground gas pipelines
summary: These unmanned ground vehicles are being adapted to navigate narrow underground gas pipelines and tunnels, where Russian forces have attempted to bypass frontline defenses.
details: Ukraine is developing a new class of combat robots specifically designed to operate inside underground gas pipelines. These unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) will perform reconnaissance and combat missions in spaces too narrow for conventional military machinery. Russian troops have repeatedly attempted to bypass frontline defenses using such infrastructure, including a 1.2-meter diameter gas pipeline near Kupiansk.

The project is being carried out by specialists from Ukraine's 2nd National Guard Corps, Khartiia, specifically their Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment. This initiative follows Operation Veles, an underground assault where Ukrainian soldiers advanced over 15 kilometers through pipeline infrastructure. Khartiia claims this operation resulted in over 100 enemy soldiers killed and 30 captured.

The commander of Lava's ground robotic system battalion, 'Matematyk', emphasized that this project addresses a new category of warfare requiring a different approach from conventional battlefield robotics. The machines are being adapted from existing ground robots to be compact enough for narrow pipelines while retaining military capabilities.

Commercially available underground machinery is typically designed for construction, drilling, and tunneling, not combat. Khartiia is developing several robotic systems to overcome these limitations, aiming to send machines into dangerous underground environments for reconnaissance, confronting enemy positions, or clearing areas.

The need for these robots stems from unusual battlefield developments near Kupiansk, where both sides have used underground infrastructure. Russian forces previously exploited the pipeline network beneath the Oskil River to infiltrate Ukrainian territory. Human operations in these environments restrict visibility, complicate communications, and limit maneuvering.

Ukraine has increasingly relied on unmanned military systems as battlefield terrain proves challenging. This includes deploying AI-controlled drones capable of independently identifying and attacking targets. The country is also exploring unmanned systems beyond conventional aerial platforms to adapt to evolving warfare.
